extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of constitutional/political theory, policymakers, and informed public interested in the British parliamentary system
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting evaluative standards for how a parliamentary (especially British) system should be constituted and should perform its functions — e.g., representation, election of ministers, legislation, teaching, expression, and informing the nation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation of Parliament members
rubrics_metrics.description: The mass of a Parliament ought to be men of moderate sentiments, or they will elect an immoderate Ministry, and enact violent laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If Parliament's members are immoderate, it tends to produce immoderate Ministries and violent legislation. Moderation (a general, middling sentiment among members) is a necessary condition for the bare possibility of parliamentary government; without it a deliberative assembly will become a 'various compound of all sorts of violence.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Compulsory (geographical) constituencies over voluntary constituencies
rubrics_metrics.description: If the above reasoning be sound, compulsory constituencies are necessary, voluntary constituencies destructive; the optional transferability of votes is not a salutary aid, but a ruinous innovation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Voluntary constituencies permit caucuses and special interest organisations to form self-selected electorates (chapels, congregations, etc.), produce party committees that select and chain representatives, and create opportunities for latent manipulators to be the real rulers. The text gives examples of caucuses picking unknown men and of chapel-based vote-transfer practices. The author's warning: voluntary constituencies undermine independence and moderation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence of members from constituency control
rubrics_metrics.description: A voluntary constituency will nearly always be a despotic constituency; members will be like the minister of a dissenting congregation — if he does not preach the set doctrine, he is dismissed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Members must retain extrinsic independence from tightly-organised constituencies. Where constituencies are 'in earnest' (unified around doctrine), they will 'look after' their representative to ensure he adheres to their mandates, producing representatives 'chained to that committee and pledged to party violence.' This is an anti-pattern: representatives become delegates of their organisers rather than independent deliberators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elect the Ministry well
rubrics_metrics.description: One of five essential functions: the House of Commons must elect a Ministry well — choose rulers as the people wish rulers to be chosen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parliament should align with public opinion in appointing and retaining governments. Example: despite near parity in 1859, Parliament retained Lord Palmerston because the 'common element' (moderates from both parties) supported him. If Parliament reliably selects what the nation wants, it performs this function satisfactorily; otherwise public grievance and powerful leagues will arise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislate well (pass laws as the nation wishes)
rubrics_metrics.description: One of five essential functions: the House of Commons must legislate well — pass laws that accord with national will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Though parliamentary procedure may be faulty (e.g., the committee of the whole House dealing with long bills producing misplaced clauses), the essence of legislation can be separated from such accidents. Subject to certain defects, Parliament should produce legislation that reflects the formed opinion of the country. The machinery of legislation is criticised as odious and in need of improvement, but the criterion focuses on whether laws match popular will.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach the nation well (the teaching function)
rubrics_metrics.description: One of five essential functions: the House of Commons must teach the nation well — elevate public opinion by presenting high truths in an accessible way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the task Parliament does worst. The Prime Minister (head-master) has special responsibility to set a high tone and embody distinct policies and truths. Teaching in Parliament must be popular, concrete, and short — the 'highest truth which the people will bear' — and avoid lowering standards (example: Palmerston's genial but lowening influence). Debates should uplift rather than merely entertain or flatter contemporary sentiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Express the nation's will well (the expressive/lyrical function)
rubrics_metrics.description: One of five essential functions: Parliament must express the nation's will well — pour out the characteristic heart of the nation in words when words (not laws) are wanted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parliament is effective at articulating the national mood, especially on foreign matters where legislation is not possible. Its debates act as a unique voice of a free people; expressing national opinion faithfully is part of what makes a parliamentary system 'free government.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Bring matters to the nation's attention (informing function / representation of special classes)
rubrics_metrics.description: One of five essential functions: bring before the nation the ideas, grievances, and wishes of special classes; the informing function (distinct from teaching) is to present sectional, neglected, or new facts and views.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parliament should provide spokesmen for special trades and classes so that their particular notions and grievances are seen and examined (e.g., shipping, wool, linen trades). Neglected classes may contain truths valuable to national policy; thus admitting working-class advocates improves Parliament's informational quality. Visible advocates also address the 'gross appearance' of representation: if artisans have no obvious spokesmen, public belief in imperfect representation will persist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation should reflect current economic and geographic realities
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a grave objection that the Parliamentary constitution gives much power to regions of past greatness and refuses equal power to regions of present greatness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The existing over-weighting of southern and landed districts (set when those regions were dominant) fails to reflect modern industrial concentrations (the North). Correcting regional malapportionment is a major cause of reformist pressure; the political salience of manufacturing and urban centres should be recognised in representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive dominance of the landed interest (class bias)
rubrics_metrics.description: Parliament leans too much to the opinions of the landed interest: county members often put rent and land interests ahead of others (example: the Cattle Plague Act rushed through the House).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: County representation often returns landed proprietors and excludes able men from other counties (no 'free trade' in the agricultural mind). While some aristocratic presence is defensible and useful for national cohesion, excessive influence of the landed interest skews legislation and privileges sectional interests; the danger is despotism if the landed interest were cleverer or better represented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance representation of property and mind (composition of Parliament)
rubrics_metrics.description: Parliament represents mind coupled with property; it is not desirable to have a representation of pure mind, but the country could bear 'a little more mind' — i.e., a modest increase in intellectual representation is acceptable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The composition should mirror the nation's habits of deference, which currently give weight to property; however, some pruning of 'opulent dulness' and a slight increase in capable, intellectual members would be beneficial without overturning the representative character rooted in property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid wholesale simultaneous ministerial changes (stability in executive personnel)
rubrics_metrics.description: All our administrators go out together when Ministries change, and this practice produces three great evils: (1) it brings in untried persons to preside over policy; (2) it keeps present ministers indifferent to their tasks; (3) it may cause mischievous changes of policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frequent or wholesale changes of departmental heads undermine expertise and continuity. Example: Lord Cranborne suddenly becoming Indian Secretary without prior experience; difficulty of assembling a balanced ministry likened to a Chinese puzzle. Continuity of moderate competence often better serves long-term tasks (e.g., military preparation, technological adoption) than rapid oscillations of leadership. Hence, excessive simultaneous turnover is a defect to be avoided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guard against frequent elections driven by organised constituencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Voluntary constituencies and devoted electorates would exact frequent elections; earnest constituencies would not like to keep their representatives long and would enjoin annual elections, which would undermine stability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short-lived Parliaments weaken ministerial independence; a septennial (longer) Parliament reduces manipulative pressure. Frequent elections are an anti-pattern arising from organised, doctrinal constituencies and from constituency-makers who prefer frequent contests to maintain control.
